Periodic Table of Elemental Peels

Jeromie Beasley · hydrogen to darmstadtium · v2.2 · Codex comparison edition, 23 November 2026
peel step z = IEₖ₊₁ / IEₖ · reflection Γ = (z − 1)/(z + 1) · the loop wall Γ² = ½ · z = 3 + 2√2 = 5.828427

Each element is read as a chain of its own removal energies. Every step of the chain is a reflection on one disk, and the loop wall splits the disk in two. An element's address is where two of its steps fall: the anion rung, from the electron affinity to the first ionisation energy, and the first opening of its noble-gas core. Of 3,570 steps from hydrogen to astatine, eight lie outside the wall, and every one is the first opening of a core. The same archive carries the ladders on from radon to darmstadtium; they are drawn here as a separate extension, mostly theoretical, and none of their steps is counted in the 3,570.

The address of an element is a pair: its anion rung and the first opening of its noble-gas core, each inside or outside the wall. Seven addresses occur in the plotted v1 baseline. An unscored affinity can mean an unbound state, an unresolved observation, or an estimate excluded from that baseline; each drawer gives its evidence status.

Each strand follows one noble-gas core across the table: the ratio of the step that first opens that core, element by element. The gold line is the wall. Every strand starts outside the wall and crosses inward after one to four elements: helium after carbon, the other four cores after their first element.

All 3,570 removal steps (dots) and 65 anion rungs (rings) on the reflection disk: distance from the centre is Γ, angle is atomic number. The gold circle is the wall Γ² = ½. Eight ordinary removal steps and 53 of the 65 baseline anion rungs lie outside it.

The anion rung read as chemistry. Hardness η = (IE − EA)/2 is the stone; electronegativity χ = (IE + EA)/2 is the pull. The rung's reflection is Γ₀ = η/χ, and electrophilicity ω = χ²/2η. On the wall, χ/η = 1/Γ₀ = √2 and ω = η. This dimensionless descriptor uses half-hardness. The quadratic E(x) = E₀ − χx + ηx² matching the two threshold energies has its formal minimum at x = χ/(2η), or 1/√2 on the wall. Actual charge uptake requires a reservoir and a measured response. Above the plotted line are 53 of 65 baseline anion rungs; 12 lie below.

The optical comparison uses the same numerical half-power threshold: the mean returned power |Γ|² of each element's surface across 400–700 nm (optical constants from the vacuum-disk paper, refractiveindex.info). All 35 metals sit above |Γ|² = ½ and none of the 6 non-metals do.

Walter Russell's octaves run from one inert gas to the next: tones 1+, 2+, 3+, apex 4, then 3−, 2−, 1−. Each element sits at the height of its anion-rung Γ₀²; the gold line is the wall. The P→S, As→Se and Sb→Te rows turn inward from 3− to 2−. Oxygen stays outside at 2− and fluorine turns inside at 1−. Bismuth (3−) is outside and astatine (1−) is inside; polonium (2−) has a preliminary inside reading and no scored v1 point.

The elements on one spiral, after Russell's spiral: one turn per period, each element at its place in the period, and its distance from the axis set by a reflection of its own chain. The translucent gold cylinder is the wall, radius 1/√2. Drag to turn, scroll to zoom, click an element to open it. This is a way of drawing the same numbers, not a claim about Russell's own chart.

Strip the same number of electrons from two isobars and their ground-mass gap moves by the difference of their removal energies: Q(q + 1) − Q(q) = IH − IL. Starting from each measured neutral gap and adding the archived thresholds one charge at a time gives the curves below. Above zero the first atom is heavier and decays toward the second; below zero the direction reverses. The bare ends agree with the storage-ring decays of bare rhenium-187 and bare dysprosium-163 and with the lead–thallium reversal.

The same table read on other shapes. The disk is one choice of shape; here every removal step and anion rung is carried onto a triangle, square, diamond or hexagon, by a chart that keeps angles (Schwarz–Christoffel) or one stretched out to the faces. Below, each element's two books (anion rung and first core opening) sit on the diamond, one edge per book; and a table gives how well each shape groups the columns.

The address on the diamond

Which shape groups the columns

Each element's first 8 removal steps are its books; on each shape, its nearest element is found by that shape's own distance. Hydrogen to astatine, 77 elements with 8 steps. Every shape groups the columns far better than the raw energies do (0.05). The triangle family, which reads only the shape of the ladder, scores highest, but no shape beats the circle by more than its bootstrap spread. Script PT-SHAPES-01B on the element-paper/loop-wall branch.

Twenty atoms do not fill in the plain order. In ten, the electron moves into the d shell of its own row; in ten more, an n + l tie between two shells is broken toward d, and at lawrencium toward 7p. Tiles carry a small mark: d for a move in the d row, t for a tie. The strips show each d row's first peel step z₁ = IE₂/IE₁, movers filled.
